scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that values testing understanding while arguing facts remain essential; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Students can sometimes memorise many facts without truly understanding any of them.
Some people recommend that educators should assess students not on their grasp of facts but on their ability to explain the ideas and concepts behind them.
I agree that understanding matters most, but I believe facts and ideas must both be part of any fair assessment.
First, judging students by their understanding reveals far more than testing facts alone.
Someone who can explain why something happens shows real and lasting knowledge.
For example, a learner who explains why the seasons change understands more than one who only names them.
This shows that the ability to explain ideas is a deeper sign of genuine learning.
Tests of pure memory often reward cramming that students forget within days.
Assessing understanding also encourages students to think rather than merely repeat.
To this extent, the recommendation rightly values comprehension over memorised facts.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why facts are still needed

sentences.text: Second, however, ideas cannot truly be understood or explained without some facts to build on.
A student cannot explain a historical event without first knowing the basic facts of what happened.
Consider a science learner who must know certain facts before she can explain any larger theory.
Such cases show that facts and understanding depend on each other and cannot be separated.
Ignoring facts entirely could leave students confident but mistaken about what is actually true.
Good assessment, therefore, should test both what students know and how well they understand it.
Facts and ideas, then, belong together in any fair test.
In conclusion, assessing students on their understanding is wiser than testing facts alone.
But facts cannot be ignored, since ideas can only be explained on a base of real knowledge.
The best assessment measures both the facts students know and the understanding they can show.
